translation:
Harishran Jagmohanbhai writes about Dhanora: Harma Ba's Deliverance.

_Dhanora gaame sarovar paal, sooko peepal leelo thaay, Ratansingh mukhi-nu naam, apang Harmaabaanaa thaay kaam, Sooku sarovar jal bharyu, apangpanu to sahaje talyu._ (In the village of Dhanora, by the lake's bank, the dry peepal tree turned green; through the name of Ratansinh the headman (mukhi), the deed was done for the disabled Harmaba; the dry lake filled with water, and her disability was easily removed.)

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, together with his company of saints, was going to the abode of his own Sadguru Gopalji on the occasion of the Sharad Nisha (autumn full-moon night) festival. It was afternoon, and the heat of the Otara-Chitra season was blazing. The saints were drenched in sweat. The devotee-saints Santdas, Gopaldas, Devdas, and Ramdas walked along, singing kirtan (hymns) of Hari and the praises of Ram. Before reaching Choranda, everyone silently wished in their hearts to rest for a short while. But who would say so aloud? Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, knowing everyone's mind, said, "Santdas, if it is the wish of the saintly devotees, let us settle here on the bank of this lake." Gopalji of Chanderiya thought: since this thought has come to the Sadguru's mind, surely the fortune of this land is about to awaken. As the Sadguru wishes! But while spreading a seat for the Sadguru, it was noticed that the peepal tree was dry and gave no shade.

If they had sat in the shade, the mind would have found ease. Santdas said, "One who has the shade of Sadguru Jivanji - what further need has he of any other shade?" Devidas said, "We are truly most fortunate to have received the good fortune of living in the Sadguru's shade." Rupa Bhagat said - _Taruvar sarvar sant jan, chautha varse maih, Parmarath ke kaarane, chaaro dhariya deh_ (Trees, lakes, saints, and, fourth, the rain-cloud - these four have taken bodily form for the sake of others' welfare). Nana Gopal said, "Your sakhi (couplet) is true, but here the opposite seems to be the case." Santdas said, "How does it seem opposite?" Nana Gopal said, "A tree should be green, but this peepal is utterly dry; if it were green and leafy it would give good shade, and if the lake were full of water, people and animals could quench their thirst. Yet here, even though the monsoon has passed, the peepal stays dry and the lake is empty. Now, explain that!" A doubt lingered in Devidas's mind, so he said to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, "O Bapji, how could this be? Someone will surely say, what kind of company of saints is this, sitting under a tree with no shade, settling by a lake with no water!"

As this conversation was going on, four men arrived carrying axes and said, "O sadhus and saints, we must cut down this peepal. Ratansinh the mukhi (headman) has sent us for it. By evening the mukhi will ask us about the work, so let us do it - please move your camp from here." Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj said, "Brothers, in the Gita the Lord says, 'Among trees, I am the peepal tree' - therefore the peepal is sacred and must not be cut." The leader of the labourers said, "Maharaj, that would be right if the peepal were green. But here the peepal is dry." Just then the eyes of Santdas and Devidas moved over the tree, and they saw green shoots sprouting on the upper branches. They said, "If the peepal is green, then surely it must not be cut, brother." The leader of the labourers said, "Yes, a green peepal should not be cut, but this one has stayed dry through the whole monsoon." Santdas said, "Brother, just look up for a moment." Hearing this, everyone looked up at the branches and saw the shoots that had sprouted. The poor labourers fell into confusion, not knowing what answer to give now, for they were bound by their own word to the saints that a green peepal must not be cut.

The foreman (mukadam) said, "The whole village knows the lake's peepal is dry - you are being lazy in your work. So let me go and tell the mukhi that the peepal is green and that the Maharaj of this company of saints refuses to let it be cut. Let the mukhi come and do as he wishes - our task is done." He said to Jivanji Maharaj, "Bapji, please wait a while - I must go and tell the mukhi why the peepal has not been cut." Jivanji Maharaj said, "As the merciful Lord wills."

Reaching Ratansinh's house, the labourers' foreman began, "Bapu, we labourers went to the outskirts (bhagol) to cut down the dry peepal." The mukhi said, "Yes - have you cut it and stacked the logs properly so they don't scatter?" The foreman said, "No, Bapu." The mukhi said, "Then why have you come here?" The foreman said, "Bapu, when we went to cut it, a company of saints had settled there to rest. When we asked them to move away, their mahant (leader) said that according to dharma a peepal must not be cut." The mukhi said, "Yes, according to dharma a green peepal is not cut - but this one was dry, so you should have said it may be cut." "Bapu, we said just that: if it were green it should not be cut, but since it is dry, Mukhi Bapu has ordered it cut. Then what was the problem, you ask? Bapu, while we were saying this, one of the men in their company said the upper branch showed green shoots, and when we all looked, we truly saw green shoots on the upper branch. Then the mahant said, 'Now, being green, the peepal must not be cut, according to dharma.' We said, wait, let us go and tell Mukhi Bapu - they agreed to do as told." The mukhi said, "Can such a thing be? The whole village knows the peepal has dried up." The foreman said, "Bapu, see it with your own eyes and tell us, and we will do as you say." The mukhi said, "This just doesn't sink into my head. Go, tell two or four of the village leaders that they are to come with the mukhi to the outskirts."

The foreman went off, and the mukhi, putting on his coat (dagalo) and tying a turban (moryu) on his head, turned toward the house and said, "Listen, I am going to the outskirts for a while - I just cannot understand how a dry peepal could turn green." His wife said, "What did you say - the lake's peepal at the outskirts has turned green? That cannot be, what are you saying?" In the house their daughter Harma was listening to this. Harma had been disabled from birth; the mukhi had tried much medicine and treatment, as well as charms and threads (dora dhaga), but nothing had helped. Harma said, "Where have Father and Mother gone, what were they saying?" Her mother told her that a company of saints was seated under the dry peepal, and that the peepal had turned green. "Oh Mother! Please take me for their darshan - may my suffering be removed through the saints." Her mother said, "Child, when your father returns I will speak to him. If it is God's will, good things will happen."

Meanwhile the mukhi sent word to the other leaders to come with him to the outskirts. They said, "Now why should we go there?" The foreman explained that the peepal on the lake's bank had turned green, with shoots sprouting on its branch. They said, "What, can such a thing be? Come, we are coming." This news passed from ear to ear through the village of Dhanora, and the villagers gathered at the outskirts to see this wonder. They saw the saints singing the praises of Hari, and shoots visible on the topmost branch of the peepal.

People began saying among themselves, "Believe it or not, these are true saints." Someone said, "No, no - this Bapji is a worker of miracles. We should ask him why water does not stay in our lake - if the lake held water, cattle and livestock would all have the comfort of it. This is like the Ganga arriving at our very doorstep - why go elsewhere to wash our hands?" Someone said, "There is a great sorrow right in Mukhi Baba's own household - Harma is disabled, we should ask for a remedy so her disability may go." Another said, "Don't be so eager - if Mukhi Baba wants to ask, let him; what is it to us?" A third said, "Stop your cleverness, listen to what Mukhi Bapa has to say." Putting the mukhi in front, the crowd of villagers went to the outskirts; a great flood of people, young and old, had surged there. The mukhi and the leaders signalled the crowd to stand back, and they themselves reached the bank of the lake where the company of saints was seated.

Seeing Jivanji, they said, "Jai, jai, Bapji." Jivanji said, "Tell me, why have you come?" The mukhi said, "This peepal was dry." Jivanji said, "Yes, the peepal was dry." The mukhi said, "Bapji, now green shoots have sprouted on top." Jivanji said, "Yes, green shoots have sprouted on top." The mukhi said, "Bapji, how did this happen?" Jivanji said, "By the grace of the saints the peepal has turned green. It had dried up, and water does not stay in this lake either - is that not so?" The mukhi said, "Bapji, we were about to ask why water does not stay in the lake." Jivanji said, "Because of the bones of an ungrateful person (kritaghni), this peepal had dried up and the lake does not hold water." The mukhi said, "Bapji, the peepal has indeed turned green - but if you would do something so that water remains in this lake, the suffering of the people and animals of the village would be removed." Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj said, "Santdas, go into the lake, remember the saints, and lift up one clod of earth - go, by the grace of the saints, water will appear in the lake."

_Kritadhnike haadsu peepal sooko en |_
_Kunaariko doshan lago, kahi samajhaave chen ||_
(By the bones of an ungrateful one this peepal has dried up thus; and the same blemish had fastened on the maiden - so he explained, and set their minds at ease.)

Taking the Sadguru's command upon his head, Santdas went, saying, "Wah Guru, your glory is boundless - you made the peepal green, now let us see the grace of the merciful Lord." Coming to the middle of the lake, he looked toward the Sadguru; the Sadguru's eyes were smiling. It occurred to Santdas that the Sadguru's divine play (leela) is boundless. Remembering the Sadguru, he lifted the clod of earth - and behold, a spring burst forth like a small stream! "Wah Guru, wah Sadguru!" Standing there he called out, "Say, victory to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj!" - declaring it was as if Mother Yamuna herself had appeared. Everyone's eyes saw the spring of water; the saints of the company called out, "Victory to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj! Victory to Baba Namdev Kabir!" The whole gathering took up this cry of victory, and the Sadguru's triumph resounded there.

Ratansinh the mukhi and the village folk, young and old, seeing this grace, felt themselves blessed and fulfilled. The mukhi said, "Bapji, please come into the village." Jivanji Maharaj said, "We must reach our Guru's abode, so we are in haste." Ratansinh's wife sent word to the mukhi to speak about their Harma. The mukhi remembered his daughter's suffering, told Jivanji Maharaj about Harma, and sent two people to bring her there. Joy filled Harma's heart - the peepal had turned green, the lake had filled with water. "If even lifeless things received new life through Jivanji's sacred footsteps, then I, who am a living, conscious being - my disability will surely, surely go." Those who had come seated Harma on a cot and carried her along.

Thoughts moved in Harma's mind: her body's disability would be removed - not by a physician's medicine - and her body would be freed from lying always in one place; her frame would move about freely. The wise say that to remove the disability of the mind, the darshan of the Sadguru and holy company (satsang) are necessary. "My fortune will awaken, my life will be set right" - such a wheel of thought kept turning, and then she saw the gathered crowd and the company of saints seated, singing the praises of Hari. Harmaba said, "Wah! In the company of saints everyone sings Hari's name; in this world the mind runs about in the chase of 'mine and yours,' but for a moment here it comes to rest in the remembrance and kirtan of Hari. Your darshan is purifying." The people made way for the cot carried like a palanquin. As Harma's eyes fell upon the company of saints, memories of a previous birth began to surface from her unconscious mind. It seemed to her that she had had this darshan before, though her memory could not fully support it - she could not quite recall it. It came to her like the memory of Kubja, who was with the child-cowherds (baalgopal) when Krishna went to Mathura at the time of the slaying of Kansa.

The eyes of Santdas, Gopaldas, and Devdas turned toward Sadguru Jivanji - how would the nectar-stream of compassion flow from this ocean of compassion? Seeing Harma's condition, they said inwardly, "Your suffering will go, and through the Sadguru's darshan happiness will come; now the glory of the gracious Ramji will resound throughout your life." Sadguru Jivandas said, "Santdas, bring water from the lake." Santdas went to fetch it. Sadguru Jivandas then told the story of Shabari: every day, before the sages went for their morning bath, Shabari would clear away thorns and pebbles from the path leading from Sage Matang's ashram to Pampa lake, keeping it free of thorns. This Shabari was a Bhil (tribal) princess who, distressed by the violence [animal slaughter] that would take place at her wedding, left her family and lived in Sage Matang's ashram. Because of this, the sages, using the entry of an 'untouchable' girl into the ashram as a pretext, kept Sage Matang apart from all of them, claiming that his body had made the water of Pampa lake impure; but Sage Matang declared the remedy - that it would be purified by the touch of Shabari's feet.

_Adhik badhaavat aapse, jan mahima Raghuveer, Sabari pad raj pasarte, shuddh thayo salila neer._ (Raghuveer [Ram] raises the glory of his devotee even higher than his own; when the dust of Shabari's feet spread there, the water became pure.)

Santdas came and handed the water-pot (kamandal) to Sadguru Jivan. Calling out "Victory to Namdev Kabir," he sprinkled the water from the kamandal on Harma and gave her some to drink, and by this Harma's disability was removed. Gopaldas called out, "Victory to Sadguru Jivanji!" and the crowd gave a joyous response. (It occurred to Ratansinh the mukhi to give Harma into Jivanji's service, and he consulted the other village elders about this.)

Feeling her disability lifted from her body, Harma stood up and, prostrating full-length (sashtang dandvat) before Sadguru Jivanji, said, "I am the maidservant of your feet - grant me your service birth after birth. O Sadguru, remove the hardship of all my lives to come." Harma said, "I have already wedded myself to you in mind, deed, and word - fulfil the longing of all my lives," and she spoke this sakhi (couplet):

_Harmaabaai harakhiyaan Jeevan darshan paay, Sharir saanso metiyo, bhayo gyaan prakaash. Gyaan prakaashi guru milaa, so kyon bisari jaay, Jab Govind krupa karai, tab guru miliya aay._ (Harmabai rejoiced upon receiving the darshan of Jivan; the anguish of the body was erased, and the light of knowledge dawned. Having found a guru who illumines knowledge, how could he ever be forgotten? Only when Govind [God] bestows his grace does one come to find the guru.)

Hearing this sakhi, Jivanji was pleased and said, "This woman is full of devotion. The merciful Lord will fulfil your longing." Harma said, "Lord, I have wedded myself to you in mind and word - accept me. Know me as the maidservant of your feet and grant me service at your feet."

Jivanji said, "We are a sadhu (renunciate) and cannot accept you. Besides, we are going on pilgrimage to Jagannath and Badrinath." Harmaba said - _Tumku chhaand avar kahaan jaau, nishdin tumaari sang rahaau_ (Leaving you, where else could I go? Day and night I would remain with you).

It occurred to Ratansinh the mukhi that this Harma had received new life through Jivanji's grace: "If this is her wish, we should consult the elders and consider it. Among us Rajputs there is a custom of regarding a daughter as unlucky and putting her to death by drowning in milk (a form of female infanticide), yet even though she was disabled from birth, such a thought never once arose in my mind regarding her. On the contrary, seeing her, I always felt she was a gift of God (Paramatma) - perhaps God gave her to me to be served, since being disabled she could not be joined in marriage to anyone in society. So why should I not gladly serve her, being pleased with God's will? My heart tells me this Harma is a trust (amaanat) placed by God - why should this divine trust not be entrusted to this saint, who is the very form of God!" The village leaders also thought, "Blessed is this - Ratansinh's daughter was disabled from birth, yet he never did anything to hurt Harma's heart. Today his heart is set on entrusting her to this saint - why should we refuse? His yes is our yes as well."

After deliberating, they all began to insist and plead with Jivanji to accept Harma. Jivanji looked within (antardarshan), and the future Uda community became visible to him. He said, "We will accept her when we return from pilgrimage." It occurred to Santdas, Gopaldas, Devdas, and Ramdas: rather than wandering about in the company of saints like this, if their family and community had one settled place, they could enjoy the benefit of the Sadguru's company day and night. "Wah Guru, wah Sadguru, your divine play is boundless."
